```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
library(readr); library(readxl); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(knitr)

design_csv <- "data/sample_design.csv"
raw_xlsx   <- "results/dada2/raw_counts_dada2.xlsx"
perm_csv   <- "results/dada2/permanova_by_level.csv"
ancom_xlsx <- "results/dada2/ancombc2_results_by_level.xlsx"
fig_dir    <- "figures/dada2"

fmt   <- function(x, d = 0) format(round(x, d), big.mark = ",", nsmall = d)
pfmt  <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, formatC(p, format = "e", digits = 1), formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
ranks <- c("Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species")
read_book <- function(f) { s <- excel_sheets(f); setNames(lapply(s, \(x) read_excel(f, sheet = x)), s) }
```

This tutorial analyses 16S rRNA gene data processed with nf-core/ampliseq
[1, 2] in R. It has three parts:

* **Sections 2–11:** the DADA2 [3] / SILVA 138.2 [4] taxonomy.
* **Section 12:** the same analyses with the QIIME 2 [5] / SILVA 138
  taxonomy.
* **Section 13:** functions predicted by PICRUSt2 [6].

Each section shows a short code example, the result, and a brief
interpretation.

**Data:** the mothur MiSeq SOP faecal samples from one mouse
[7, 8]:

* **Early:** E01–E09, days 0–9 after weaning;
* **Late:** L01–L10, days 141–150.

---

# 1. Upstream processing with nf-core/ampliseq

## 1.1 Pipeline and settings

nf-core/ampliseq 2.18.0 is a Nextflow [9] pipeline from nf-core
[10]. It processed 2 × 250 bp MiSeq reads of the 16S V4 region
[7] as follows:

| Step | Tool | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| Primer removal | Cutadapt | skipped: the MiSeq SOP reads contain no primer |
| Filtering, denoising, merging, chimera removal | DADA2 [3] | auto-truncation at median quality 25 (≥ 75% of reads kept); maxEE 2; per-sample inference |
| ASV clustering | VSEARCH [11] | 97% identity: each feature is a cluster of near-identical ASVs |
| Taxonomy 1 | DADA2 `assignTaxonomy` + `addSpecies` | SILVA 138.2, bootstrap ≥ 50 |
| Taxonomy 2 | QIIME 2 `classify-sklearn` [12] | SILVA 138 |
| Function | PICRUSt2 [6] | EC, KO, MetaCyc |
| Output | phyloseq [13] | `dada2_phyloseq.rds`, `qiime2_phyloseq.rds` |

The pipeline runs as a SLURM job on the MSU HPCC, following the ICER and
MSU Bioinformatics Core format [14, 15]. The job itself
runs only the Nextflow head process (1 CPU, 4 GB); Nextflow submits each
pipeline step as its own SLURM job.

**1. Create a configuration file.** Create `icer.config` with a text editor
(`nano icer.config`) containing:

```groovy
process {
    executor = 'slurm'
}
```

**2. Create the job script** `run_ampliseq.sh` (`nano run_ampliseq.sh`):

```bash
#!/bin/bash --login
#SBATCH --job-name=ampliseq
#SBATCH --time=24:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=4GB
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --output=ampliseq-%j.out

# Load Nextflow
module purge
module load Nextflow

# Define the samplesheet, outdir, workdir, and config
SAMPLESHEET="$HOME/ampliseq/samplesheet.tsv"
OUTDIR="$HOME/ampliseq/results"
WORKDIR="$SCRATCH/ampliseq/work"
CONFIG="$HOME/ampliseq/icer.config"

# Run nf-core/ampliseq
nextflow pull nf-core/ampliseq
nextflow run nf-core/ampliseq -r 2.18.0 -profile singularity -work-dir $WORKDIR -resume \
--input $SAMPLESHEET \
--outdir $OUTDIR \
--FW_primer GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA --RV_primer GGACTACNVGGGTWTCTAAT \
--skip_cutadapt \
--dada_ref_taxonomy silva=138.2 \
--qiime_ref_taxonomy silva=138 \
--vsearch_cluster \
--picrust \
-c $CONFIG

# Job information and resource usage
scontrol show job $SLURM_JOB_ID
module load powertools
js -j $SLURM_JOB_ID
```

**3. Submit and monitor:**

```bash
sbatch run_ampliseq.sh
squeue -u $USER
```

The results are written to `$HOME/ampliseq/results`.

## 1.2 DADA2 and QIIME 2

**DADA2** [3] is an R package for amplicon sequence inference. Its
core algorithm learns a parametric error model from the run and then
partitions the reads into **exact amplicon sequence variants (ASVs)**. A
new ASV is split off only when its abundance is too high to be explained
by sequencing errors from a more abundant sequence. DADA2 also merges read
pairs, removes chimeras and assigns taxonomy. In ampliseq it produces the
feature table and the first taxonomy.

**QIIME 2** [5] is a plugin-based platform covering the whole
microbiome workflow: import, denoising (through DADA2 or Deblur), taxonomy,
diversity and statistics. In ampliseq it provides the second taxonomy,
through its q2-feature-classifier plugin [12], and the removal
of organelle sequences.

**Same in function and algorithm.**

* **Same task.** Both assign a taxonomic lineage to each 16S feature from a
  reference database (here SILVA).
* **Same algorithm family.** Both use a **naive Bayes *k*-mer classifier**:
  each sequence is broken into short words (*k*-mers), and the most
  probable reference lineage given those words is chosen.
* **Same output logic.** Both assign the lineage rank by rank, attach a
  confidence value, and stop at the first rank whose confidence falls below
  the cut-off, leaving lower ranks unassigned.

**Different in function and algorithm.**

| | DADA2 `assignTaxonomy` / `addSpecies` | QIIME 2 `classify-sklearn` |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithm | RDP naive Bayesian classifier [16] | multinomial naive Bayes (scikit-learn) [12] |
| *k*-mer features | 8-mers | 7-mers (hashed) |
| Confidence measure | bootstrap: share of 100 resamples of the *k*-mers that give the same lineage | posterior probability of the lineage |
| Default cut-off used | bootstrap ≥ 50 | confidence ≥ 0.7 |
| Training reference | full-length 16S sequences | reference reads cut to the amplified region (515F/806R), i.e. region-specific |
| Species level | separate exact-match step (`addSpecies`, 100% identity) | from the reference label, under the same confidence rule |
| Scope in ampliseq | denoising, read merging, chimera removal and taxonomy | taxonomy and taxon filtering only |

**Practical consequence.** The two tools classify the same features, so
any result that does not use taxonomy is identical between them. Results
at a given rank can differ: through the algorithm (bootstrap vs posterior
confidence, full-length vs region-specific training) and through the
reference release used in this run (SILVA 138.2 for DADA2, SILVA 138 for
QIIME 2; Section 1.3). Section 12 compares the two.

## 1.3 SILVA 138.2

**SILVA** [4] is a curated database of aligned small- and large-subunit
rRNA gene sequences from Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, with a manually
curated taxonomy. Release **138.2** (11 July 2024) [17] changed
three things that matter here:

* **Reference set.** 510,495 SSU Ref NR99 sequences, made non-redundant at
  99% identity.
* **Nomenclature.** Genus and phylum names follow LPSN (synchronised to
  April 2023). Phyla therefore carry their validly published names:
  *Bacillota* (formerly Firmicutes), *Pseudomonadota* (Proteobacteria) and
  *Actinomycetota* (Actinobacteriota). *Lactobacillus* is split into the
  genera of the 2020 reclassification [18].
* **Taxonomy ranks.** Every prokaryote has a standard six-rank taxonomy.
  Unassigned positions are labelled *Incertae Sedis* instead of
  "uncultured".

**Database choice in ampliseq.** ampliseq 2.18.0 downloads and formats the
reference named by a parameter, as `database=version` [2]:

| Parameter | Built-in choices | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--dada_ref_taxonomy` (DADA2) | **16S/18S:** SILVA (132, 138 = 138.1, 138.2), GTDB (R05–R11), SBDI-GTDB, RDP 18, Greengenes2 (2024.09), PR2 (protists). **ITS:** UNITE (fungi, all eukaryotes). **CO1 / nifH:** COIDB, MIDORI2, Zehr nifH | `sbdi-gtdb=R11-RS232-1` |
| `--qiime_ref_taxonomy` (QIIME 2) | SILVA 138 (99%), Greengenes2 (2022.10, 2024.09), Greengenes 13_8 (85%, for testing only) | none (QIIME 2 classification is optional) |

* **Our choice.** This run selected `--dada_ref_taxonomy silva=138.2`,
  the newest SILVA, and `--qiime_ref_taxonomy silva=138`. SILVA 138 is the
  newest SILVA offered for QIIME 2, which is why the two classifiers use
  different releases.
* **Custom references.** A custom database can be supplied instead
  (`--dada_ref_tax_custom`, `--qiime_ref_tax_custom`).
* **Primer-trimmed reference.** `--cut_dada_ref_taxonomy` trims the DADA2
  reference to the amplified region; it was not used here.

For `silva=138.2`, ampliseq uses the DADA2-formatted release
[19]:

* `silva_nr99_v138.2_toSpecies_trainset.fa.gz` for `assignTaxonomy`;
* `silva_v138.2_assignSpecies.fa.gz` for `addSpecies`.

In this dataset all 178 features were classified to Order, 99 to Genus and
23 to Species.

The R analysis uses phyloseq [13], microViz [20], microbiome
[21], vegan [22], ANCOMBC [23] and ggpicrust2
[24].

# 2. Sample design

```r
library(phyloseq); library(microViz)
ps     <- readRDS("results/phyloseq/dada2_phyloseq.rds")
design <- read.csv("data/sample_design.csv")            # sample_id, time, day
design$time <- factor(design$time, levels = c("Early", "Late"))   # Early = reference
sample_data(ps) <- sample_data(data.frame(design, row.names = design$sample_id))  # names must match
```

```{r design}
design <- read_csv(design_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c("Early", "Late")))
design |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(Samples = n(), IDs = paste(first(sample_id), "–", last(sample_id)),
            Days = paste(min(day), "–", max(day))) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 1. Sample design (data/sample_design.csv)")
```

All samples come from **one mouse**. Every effect is reported as *Late vs
Early*. The Mock community sample is excluded from all statistics.

---

# 3. Raw abundance (DADA2)

```r
ps <- ps |>
  subset_taxa(Kingdom %in% "Bacteria" & !Order %in% "Chloroplast" & !Family %in% "Mitochondria") |>
  tax_fix()                                               # fill missing names from parent rank
ps_genus <- ps |> tax_agg(rank = "Genus") |> ps_get()    # one table per level
```

```{r raw}
raw <- read_book(raw_xlsx)
samples <- design$sample_id
per_sample <- tibble(sample_id = samples,
                     Reads_raw = colSums(as.matrix(raw$features_unfiltered[, samples])),
                     Reads_filtered = colSums(as.matrix(raw$features_filtered[, samples]))) |>
  left_join(design, by = "sample_id")
tot_flt <- sum(per_sample$Reads_filtered)
lapply(ranks, function(r) {
  d <- raw[[r]]
  reads <- sum(as.matrix(d[, samples]))
  tibble(Level = r, Taxa = nrow(d), Reads = fmt(reads),
         `% of reads` = round(100 * reads / tot_flt, 1),
         `Most abundant` = paste(d |> arrange(desc(total_reads)) |> slice_head(n = 3) |> pull(!!r), collapse = "; "))
}) |> bind_rows() |>
  kable(caption = "Table 2. Taxa and reads per level (results/dada2/raw_counts_dada2.xlsx)")
n_unf <- nrow(raw$features_unfiltered); n_flt <- nrow(raw$features_filtered)
n_des <- sum(rowSums(as.matrix(raw$features_unfiltered[, samples])) > 0)
lib_min <- per_sample |> slice_min(Reads_filtered, n = 1)
lib_max <- per_sample |> slice_max(Reads_filtered, n = 1)
```

* **Features.** Of `r n_unf` features, `r n_unf - n_des` occur only in the
  Mock sample and `r n_des - n_flt` are organelles. That leaves
  **`r n_flt` features** and **`r fmt(tot_flt)` reads**, from
  `r fmt(lib_min$Reads_filtered)` (`r lib_min$sample_id`) to
  `r fmt(lib_max$Reads_filtered)` (`r lib_max$sample_id`) per sample.
* **Classification.** All reads are classified to Order, but only 35.5% to a
  named genus. The dominant family, Muribaculaceae, has no named genera.
  Genus and species results cover the classified part of the community
  only.

---

# 4. Library size

```r
lib <- data.frame(reads = sample_sums(ps), time = sample_data(ps)$time)
wilcox.test(reads ~ time, data = lib)
```

```{r fig-library, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Reads per sample after filtering."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "04_library_sizes.png"))
```

```{r library}
lib_p <- wilcox.test(Reads_filtered ~ time, data = per_sample, exact = FALSE)$p.value
per_sample |> group_by(time) |>
  summarise(n = n(), Min = fmt(min(Reads_filtered)), Median = fmt(median(Reads_filtered)),
            Max = fmt(max(Reads_filtered))) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 3. Library size by condition")
```

Depth varies about seven-fold within groups, but not between them (Wilcoxon
p = `r round(lib_p, 2)`). Group differences are therefore not driven by
sequencing depth.

---

# 5. Alpha rarefaction

```r
otu <- t(as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"))                   # samples in rows
vegan::rarecurve(otu, step = 50)
ps_rare <- rarefy_even_depth(ps, sample.size = min(sample_sums(ps)), rngseed = 2026)
```

```{r fig-rarefaction, fig.cap = "Figure 2. Rarefaction curves; dashed line = rarefaction depth (2,092 reads)."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "05_alpha_rarefaction_curves.png"))
```

All curves plateau before 2,092 reads, so rarefying keeps nearly all
richness. Rarefied data are used only for alpha diversity [25].

---

# 6. Alpha diversity

```r
alpha <- ps_rare |>
  ps_calc_richness(rank = "unique", index = "observed") |>
  ps_calc_diversity(rank = "unique", index = "shannon") |>
  samdat_tbl()
alpha$pielou <- microbiome::evenness(ps_rare, index = "pielou")$pielou
wilcox.test(shannon_unique ~ time, data = alpha)
```

```{r fig-alpha, fig.cap = "Figure 3. Alpha diversity (rarefied to 2,092 reads); two-sided Wilcoxon p, nominal."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "06_alpha_diversity.png"))
```

* **Richness** does not differ (Observed and Chao1, p = 0.31).
* **Diversity and evenness** (Shannon, Simpson, Pielou) tend to be lower in
  Late samples (p = 0.066–0.18).

The two life stages carry similar diversity: *which* taxa dominate changes,
not how many there are.

---

# 7. Relative abundance

```r
ps_genus |> comp_barplot(tax_level = "Genus", n_taxa = 15, facet_by = "time")   # per sample
ps_genus |> tax_transform("compositional") |> ps_get() |>
  merge_samples(group = "time") |> comp_barplot(tax_level = "Genus", n_taxa = 15) # per condition
```

```{r ancom-read}
anc <- read_book(ancom_xlsx)
mean_tbl <- function(level, n = 5, a = anc) {
  a[[level]] |>
    transmute(Taxon = .data[[level]], `Early (%)` = round(mean_rel_abund_Early, 1),
              `Late (%)` = round(mean_rel_abund_Late, 1)) |>
    arrange(desc(`Early (%)` + `Late (%)`)) |>
    slice_head(n = n)
}
```

```{r fig-relab-overview, fig.cap = "Figure 4. Mean relative abundance of the 15 most abundant taxa per level, Early vs Late."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "07_relative_abundance_overview.png"))
```

```{r relab-table}
bind_rows(lapply(c("Phylum", "Family", "Genus", "Species"), function(r)
  mean_tbl(r) |> mutate(Level = r, .before = 1))) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 4. Mean relative abundance (%) of the five most abundant taxa per level.")
```

```{r fig-relab-phylum, fig.cap = "Figure 5. Phylum level, per sample."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "07_relative_abundance_samples_phylum.png"))
```

```{r fig-relab-class, fig.cap = "Figure 6. Class level, per sample."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "07_relative_abundance_samples_class.png"))
```

```{r fig-relab-order, fig.cap = "Figure 7. Order level, per sample."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "07_relative_abundance_samples_order.png"))
```

```{r fig-relab-family, fig.cap = "Figure 8. Family level, per sample."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "07_relative_abundance_samples_family.png"))
```

```{r fig-relab-genus, fig.cap = "Figure 9. Genus level, per sample."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "07_relative_abundance_samples_genus.png"))
```

```{r fig-relab-species, fig.cap = "Figure 10. Species level, per sample."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "07_relative_abundance_samples_species.png"))
```

* **Phylum.** *Bacteroidota* rises from 58% to 70% and *Bacillota* falls
  from 42% to 29%. Early samples vary more: E02 has only about 33%
  Bacteroidota.
* **Family.** *Muribaculaceae* rises from 45% to 63%; *Lachnospiraceae*
  falls from 27% to 15%, and *Oscillospiraceae* also falls.
* **Genus.** *Lactobacillus* (3% → 15%) and *Turicibacter* (1% → 8%)
  expand, while *Muricomes* and *Butyribacter* almost disappear.
* **Species** (8.5% of reads). *L. johnsonii* rises from 14% to 41%, and
  *B. caecimuris* falls from 81% to 54%.

---

# 8. Beta diversity (Bray–Curtis PCoA)

```r
ps |> tax_transform("compositional", rank = "unique") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |> ord_calc(method = "PCoA") |>
  ord_plot(colour = "time")
```

```{r fig-pcoa, fig.cap = "Figure 11. Bray–Curtis PCoA of all 163 features; point labels = day."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "08_pcoa_bray.png"))
```

* **MDS1 (49.6%) fully separates Early from Late.**
* **Early samples are dispersed:** E01 and E02 (days 0–1) lie far from E04
  and E07.
* **Late samples cluster tightly,** reflecting the post-weaning
  stabilisation described for this dataset [8].

---

# 9. PERMANOVA by level

```r
d <- ps |> tax_transform("compositional", rank = "unique") |> dist_calc("bray")
d |> dist_permanova(variables = "time", n_perms = 9999, seed = 2026) |> perm_get()  # PERMANOVA
d |> dist_bdisp(variables = "time") |> bdisp_get()                                  # PERMDISP
```

```{r permanova}
perm <- read_csv(perm_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Level = factor(Level, levels = c("All features", ranks)))
perm |>
  transmute(Level, Features, `R² (%)` = round(100 * R2, 1), p = pfmt(p), p_adj = pfmt(p_adj),
            `PERMDISP p` = pfmt(PERMDISP_p), `PERMDISP p_adj` = pfmt(PERMDISP_p_adj)) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 5. PERMANOVA and PERMDISP (Bray–Curtis, 9,999 permutations; p_adj = BH across levels).")
```

PERMANOVA [26] tests whether the group centroids differ;
PERMDISP [27] tests whether the groups differ in spread.
p-values are BH-adjusted across levels [28].

* **Condition explains 30–51% of the variation at every level** (44% for
  all features); all levels have p_adj ≤ 0.013.
* **Dispersion differs only for all features** (p = 0.003, the variable
  Early community). At every taxonomic level PERMDISP is not significant,
  so the shift is a genuine change of centroid.

---

# 10. Differential abundance (ANCOM-BC2)

```r
res <- ANCOMBC::ancombc2(data = ps, tax_level = "Genus", fix_formula = "time",
                         p_adj_method = "holm", prv_cut = 0.10, pseudo_sens = TRUE)
res$res[, c("taxon", "lfc_timeLate", "q_timeLate", "diff_timeLate", "passed_ss_timeLate")]
```

ANCOM-BC2 [23] corrects for sample-specific sampling bias and tests
each taxon's **log-fold change** (LFC, natural log, Late vs Early).

* **Settings.** q-values are Holm-adjusted [29]. The bias is estimated
  from all 163 features.
* **Pseudo-count fit.** Taxa absent from one condition are refitted with a
  pseudo-count of 1, so every taxon is tested.
* **Robust.** A result counts as robust when q < 0.05 *and* it passes the
  pseudo-count sensitivity analysis.

```{r ancom-summary}
anc$Summary |>
  select(Level, Taxa_tested, Tested_pseudocount, Not_tested, Significant_q05,
         Also_pass_sensitivity, Higher_in_Late, Higher_in_Early) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 6. ANCOM-BC2 summary per level (results/dada2/ancombc2_results_by_level.xlsx, sheet 'Summary').")
```

```{r ancom-fun}
anc_tbl <- function(r, n = 10, tab_no, a = anc, label = "") {
  a[[r]] |>
    arrange(p) |>
    slice_head(n = n) |>
    transmute(Taxon = .data[[r]],
              `Early %` = round(mean_rel_abund_Early, 2), `Late %` = round(mean_rel_abund_Late, 2),
              `Present E/L` = paste0(n_present_Early, "/", n_present_Late),
              LFC = round(lfc, 2), q = pfmt(q), `Wilcoxon p` = pfmt(wilcox_p_nominal),
              Robust = significant,
              Fit = ifelse(ancombc2_fit == "primary", "primary", "pseudo-count 1")) |>
    kable(caption = sprintf("Table %s. %sANCOM-BC2, %s (%d taxa; ten lowest p). Present E/L = samples with reads (of 9/10).",
                            tab_no, ifelse(label == "", "", paste0(label, ": ")), r, nrow(a[[r]])))
}
```

Each level has a table and a top-5 boxplot. The boxplots show the five
lowest-p taxa, regardless of significance, as per-sample relative
abundance.

#### Phylum

```{r ancom-phylum}
anc_tbl("Phylum", tab_no = "7a")
```

```{r fig-top5-phylum, fig.cap = "Figure 12. Top-5 phyla by ANCOM-BC2 p-value."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_phylum.png"))
```

* **Actinomycetota** is higher in Late (LFC +1.73, q = 0.012) but fails the
  sensitivity analysis.
* **Bacteroidota and Bacillota** shift in proportion (Wilcoxon p ≤ 0.016)
  with small bias-corrected LFCs (q ≥ 0.63). The shift is
  **compositional**: two phyla make up more than 99% of reads.

#### Class

```{r ancom-class}
anc_tbl("Class", tab_no = "7b")
```

```{r fig-top5-class, fig.cap = "Figure 13. Top-5 classes by ANCOM-BC2 p-value."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_class.png"))
```

**No class reaches q < 0.05.** Clostridia halves in proportion (37% → 18%)
without a significant bias-corrected change.

#### Order

```{r ancom-order}
anc_tbl("Order", tab_no = "7c")
```

```{r fig-top5-order, fig.cap = "Figure 14. Top-5 orders by ANCOM-BC2 p-value."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_order.png"))
```

* **Erysipelotrichales is robustly higher in Late** (0.1% → 2.5%; LFC
  +1.74).
* **Clostridiales is an artefact:** its LFC rests on a single Early sample,
  E01, and the sensitivity analysis flags it.

#### Family

```{r ancom-family}
anc_tbl("Family", tab_no = "7d")
```

```{r fig-top5-family, fig.cap = "Figure 15. Top-5 families by ANCOM-BC2 p-value."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_family.png"))
```

* **Erysipelotrichaceae is robust** (LFC +1.74, q = 0.016).
* **Clostridiaceae** is the same E01 artefact.
* **Oscillospiraceae** (5% → 1.2%) and the Early-only
  **Streptococcaceae** do not survive correction.

#### Genus

```{r ancom-genus}
anc_tbl("Genus", tab_no = "7e")
```

```{r fig-top5-genus, fig.cap = "Figure 16. Top-5 genera by ANCOM-BC2 p-value."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_genus.png"))
```

* **Robust, higher in Early:**
  * ***Muricomes*** (8/9 Early, 0/10 Late; LFC −3.34);
  * ***Butyribacter*** (LFC −2.05);
  * ***ASF356*** (7/9 Early, 0/10 Late).
* **Robust, higher in Late:** ***Turicibacter*** (0.9% → 8.3%; LFC +1.74).
* **Probable:** ***Lactobacillus*** (1.3% → 14%; LFC +1.83, q = 0.016) and
  ***Anaerotruncus*** fail only the sensitivity analysis.
* ***Clostridium*** is the E01 artefact.

#### Species

```{r ancom-species}
anc_tbl("Species", tab_no = "7f")
```

```{r fig-top5-species, fig.cap = "Figure 17. Top-5 species by ANCOM-BC2 p-value (% of species-classified reads)."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "10_ancombc2_top5_species.png"))
```

* ***L. johnsonii*** (7% → 43%; LFC +1.83) carries the *Lactobacillus*
  signal and is probable, not robust.
* ***S. danieliae*** and ***A. muciniphila*** (in E01 and E03 only) are
  Early-only but too rare to test reliably.

# 11. Summary of the taxonomic analysis (DADA2)

```{r robust}
bind_rows(lapply(ranks, function(r)
  anc[[r]] |> filter(significant) |>
    transmute(Level = r, Taxon = as.character(.data[[r]]), lfc = as.numeric(lfc), qv = as.numeric(q)))) |>
  transmute(Level, Taxon, LFC = round(lfc, 2), q = pfmt(qv), `Higher in` = ifelse(lfc > 0, "Late", "Early")) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 8. Robust ANCOM-BC2 differences (q < 0.05 and passed sensitivity analysis).")
```

* **Data.** Depth is balanced between conditions, and the rarefaction
  curves plateau.
* **Diversity vs composition.** Diversity is unchanged, but composition
  shifts strongly: R² = 44%, with complete separation on MDS1. The Early
  community is variable and the Late community stable.
* **Proportions.** Bacteroidota/Muribaculaceae and lactobacilli expand;
  Clostridia (Lachnospiraceae, Oscillospiraceae) contract.
* **Robust bias-corrected changes.** *Erysipelotrichaceae*/*Turicibacter*
  go up; *Muricomes*, *Butyribacter* and *ASF356* go down. *Lactobacillus*
  is a probable increase.
* **Limitations.**
  * The samples are repeated measures of **one mouse**: the p-values
    describe two periods in this animal and cannot be generalised.
  * Age is confounded with diet and housing.
  * 16S data are relative.
  * Only 35.5% of reads have a named genus.
  * Single-sample results (E01) must be checked with `Present E/L`.

  | SILVA 138.2 genus (% of all reads) | Early | Late | Wilcoxon p |
  |---|---|---|---|


## 12.4 DADA2 vs QIIME 2

```{r compare}
da_result <- function(a, r, taxon) {
  x <- a[[r]] |> filter(.data[[r]] == taxon)
  if (nrow(x) == 0) return("not assigned")
  sprintf("LFC %+.2f, q %s%s", x$lfc, pfmt(x$q),
          ifelse(x$significant, " (robust)", ifelse(x$diff, " (fails sensitivity)", "")))
}
tribble(
  ~Level,   ~DADA2,                ~QIIME2,
  "Order",  "Erysipelotrichales",  "Erysipelotrichales",
  "Family", "Erysipelotrichaceae", "Erysipelotrichaceae",
  "Genus",  "Turicibacter",        "Turicibacter",
  "Genus",  "Butyribacter",        "Lachnospiraceae_UCG-001",
  "Genus",  "ASF356",              "ASF356",
  "Genus",  "Muricomes",           "Muricomes",
  "Genus",  "Lactobacillus",       "Lactobacillus") |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(`DADA2 result` = da_result(anc, Level, DADA2),
         `QIIME 2 result` = da_result(anc_q2, Level, QIIME2)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  kable(caption = "Table 13. Key ANCOM-BC2 results with both classifiers (rows pair names of the same features; Lactobacillus differs in scope).")
```

* **Agreement.** Five of the six robust DADA2 differences are reproduced
  with identical LFCs. These classifier-independent results are the most
  defensible.
* **Differences** come from the reference taxonomy, not the statistics.
* **Recommendation.** Use DADA2 / SILVA 138.2 as the primary taxonomy, and
  QIIME 2 as a check.

# 13. Functional analysis (PICRUSt2 and ggpicrust2)

## 13.1 PICRUSt2 and ggpicrust2

**PICRUSt2** [6] predicts the genes a community carries from its 16S
sequences:

1. it places each feature in a tree of reference genomes;
2. it infers the feature's gene content from its nearest relatives;
3. it sums that content over the community, weighted by abundance and
   corrected for 16S copy number.

The output is unstratified predicted abundances of enzymes (**EC**), gene
families (**KO**) and **MetaCyc** pathways [30].

* **What it adds.** It lets an amplicon study compare functional
  *potential* between groups, test whether a taxonomic shift changes
  function, and point to functions worth validating by metagenomics or
  metabolomics.
* **In ampliseq.** ampliseq 2.18.0 runs PICRUSt2 2.6.3 with the
  PICRUSt2-SC genome database [31]; features with NSTI > 2 are
  excluded.

**ggpicrust2** [24] converts KO abundances into **KEGG** pathways
[32] and annotates them:

```r
ko <- read.delim("results/picrust/KO_pred_metagenome_unstrat_descrip.tsv", check.names = FALSE)
ko$description <- NULL                                    # KO IDs + sample columns
kegg <- ggpicrust2::ko2kegg_abundance(data = ko, method = "abundance",
                                      filter_for_prokaryotes = TRUE)
kegg_named <- ggpicrust2::pathway_annotation(data = kegg, pathway = "KEGG")
```

Each table becomes a phyloseq object with functions as "taxa", and is
analysed with the same tools as Sections 6–10:

```r
ps_fun <- phyloseq(otu_table(round(as.matrix(kegg)), taxa_are_rows = TRUE), sample_data(ps))
```

```{r fun-read}
fun_dir    <- "figures/picrust2"
fun_groups <- c("EC", "KO", "KEGG", "MetaCyc")
anc_fun    <- read_book("results/picrust2/ancombc2_results_by_group.xlsx")
fun_tbl <- function(g, tab_no) {
  anc_fun[[g]] |> arrange(p) |> slice_head(n = 10) |>
    transmute(Feature = feature, Description = substr(description, 1, 55),
              `Present E/L` = paste0(n_present_Early, "/", n_present_Late),
              LFC = round(lfc, 2), q = pfmt(q), Robust = significant,
              Fit = ifelse(ancombc2_fit == "primary", "primary", "pseudo-count 1")) |>
    kable(caption = sprintf("Table %s. ANCOM-BC2, %s (%s features; ten lowest p).",
                            tab_no, g, format(nrow(anc_fun[[g]]), big.mark = ",")))
}
```

| Dataset | Feature | Source | Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| EC | enzyme (Enzyme Commission number) | PICRUSt2 | 1,905 |
| KO | KEGG ortholog (gene family) | PICRUSt2 | 4,725 |
| KEGG | KEGG pathway | ggpicrust2, from KO | 228 |
| MetaCyc | metabolic pathway | PICRUSt2 (MinPath) | 376 |

## 13.2 Functional alpha diversity

```{r fig-fun-alpha-ec, fig.cap = "Figure 31. Functional alpha diversity, EC."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "03_alpha_diversity_EC.png"))
```

```{r fig-fun-alpha-ko, fig.cap = "Figure 32. Functional alpha diversity, KO."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "03_alpha_diversity_KO.png"))
```

```{r fig-fun-alpha-kegg, fig.cap = "Figure 33. Functional alpha diversity, KEGG pathways."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "03_alpha_diversity_KEGG.png"))
```

```{r fig-fun-alpha-metacyc, fig.cap = "Figure 34. Functional alpha diversity, MetaCyc pathways."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "03_alpha_diversity_MetaCyc.png"))
```

* **Late samples have a slightly smaller predicted repertoire.** Medians
  fall from about 1,620 to 1,410 ECs (p = 0.045), 328 to 270 MetaCyc
  pathways (p = 0.016) and 3,750 to 2,930 KOs (p = 0.055). Shannon and
  Simpson are also lower (p = 0.01–0.03).
* **The taxa lost after weaning carried unique functions,** although
  taxonomic diversity did not change.
* **KEGG pathways barely change,** because broad pathways saturate.
* **Chao1 is unreliable** on rounded predictions.

## 13.3 Functional beta diversity

```{r fig-fun-pcoa-ec, fig.cap = "Figure 35. Bray–Curtis PCoA, EC; point labels = day."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "04_pcoa_bray_EC.png"))
```

```{r fig-fun-pcoa-ko, fig.cap = "Figure 36. Bray–Curtis PCoA, KO; point labels = day."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "04_pcoa_bray_KO.png"))
```

```{r fig-fun-pcoa-kegg, fig.cap = "Figure 37. Bray–Curtis PCoA, KEGG; point labels = day."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "04_pcoa_bray_KEGG.png"))
```

```{r fig-fun-pcoa-metacyc, fig.cap = "Figure 38. Bray–Curtis PCoA, MetaCyc; point labels = day."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "04_pcoa_bray_MetaCyc.png"))
```

* **MDS1 explains 74–85% of the variation** (taxa: 50%). Functional
  profiles are redundant, so sample differences collapse onto one
  Early-to-Late gradient, and the two conditions separate in every dataset.
* **E04 and E07 (days 3 and 7) sit near the Late samples** although their
  taxonomy is Early. This is **functional redundancy**: different taxa can
  supply similar genes.

## 13.4 PERMANOVA

```{r fun-permanova}
read_csv("results/picrust2/permanova_by_group.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Group = factor(Group, levels = fun_groups)) |> arrange(Group) |>
  transmute(Dataset = Group, Features = format(Features, big.mark = ","),
            `R² (%)` = round(100 * R2, 1), p_adj = pfmt(p_adj),
            `PERMDISP p_adj` = pfmt(PERMDISP_p_adj)) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 14. PERMANOVA and PERMDISP on predicted functional profiles.")
```

Time explains **36–39%** of the functional variation (p_adj ≤ 0.004), with
no dispersion difference. Function shifts strongly with age, but slightly
less than taxonomy (44%).

## 13.5 ANCOM-BC2

ANCOM-BC2 uses the same settings as Section 10. KEGG uses the KO table to
estimate the bias.

```{r fun-ancom-summary}
anc_fun$Summary |>
  mutate(Group = factor(Group, levels = fun_groups)) |> arrange(Group) |>
  select(Group, Features_tested, Tested_pseudocount, Not_tested, Significant_q05,
         Also_pass_sensitivity, Higher_in_Late, Higher_in_Early) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 15. ANCOM-BC2 summary per functional dataset (results/picrust2/ancombc2_results_by_group.xlsx, sheet 'Summary').")
```

All 7,234 features were tested. **11 EC, 27 KO, 2 KEGG and 3 MetaCyc**
features are robust, and most are **higher in Early**. This matches the
smaller Late repertoire.

#### EC

```{r fun-ancom-ec}
fun_tbl("EC", "16a")
```

```{r fig-fun-top5-ec, fig.cap = "Figure 39. Top-5 EC numbers."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "06_top5_EC.png"))
```

All five are 8- to 16-fold lower in Late samples. They include
carboxynorspermidine synthase (polyamine biosynthesis), trans-2-enoyl-CoA
reductase (fatty-acid synthesis and fermentation) and ureidoglycine
transaminase (purine degradation).

#### KO

```{r fun-ancom-ko}
fun_tbl("KO", "16b")
```

```{r fig-fun-top5-ko, fig.cap = "Figure 40. Top-5 KOs."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "06_top5_KO.png"))
```

* **The top KOs have identical profiles** (present in all Early samples,
  absent from all Late samples). They come from the same Early-only taxa:
  **one signal, not five**.
* **Some Late-only KOs are implausible** for gut bacteria (a phycobilisome
  linker, a mitochondrial protein). They are inherited reference
  annotations.

#### KEGG

```{r fun-ancom-kegg}
fun_tbl("KEGG", "16c")
```

```{r fig-fun-top5-kegg, fig.cap = "Figure 41. Top-5 KEGG pathways."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "06_top5_KEGG.png"))
```

* **ko00196 (photosynthesis – antenna proteins)** is robust but an
  **artefact** of the phycobilisome KO.
* **Four pathways are clearly higher in Late** but fail the sensitivity
  analysis: sphingolipid signalling, aminobenzoate degradation,
  β-lactam biosynthesis and atrazine degradation.

#### MetaCyc

```{r fun-ancom-metacyc}
fun_tbl("MetaCyc", "16d")
```

```{r fig-fun-top5-metacyc, fig.cap = "Figure 42. Top-5 MetaCyc pathways."}
include_graphics(file.path(fun_dir, "06_top5_MetaCyc.png"))
```

* **Polyamine (norspermidine) biosynthesis is robustly higher in Early.**
  PWY-6565 and PWY-6562 are present in all Early samples and only 2–3 Late
  samples. This is the same signal as the EC and KO results.
* **"Firefly bioluminescence"** is another annotation artefact.

## 13.6 Summary of the functional analysis

* **Function shifts with age** (R² 36–39%), and the Late repertoire is
  slightly narrower.
* **The most consistent signal is polyamine biosynthesis,** higher in Early
  at EC, KO and MetaCyc level.
* **Functional redundancy:** E04 and E07 are taxonomically Early but
  functionally Late-like.
* **Caveats.**
  * The results are **predictions** of potential, not activity, and are
    derived from the same 163 features.
  * Identical profiles count once.
  * Implausible pathways are artefacts.
  * The one-animal limitation applies.

# 14. Tools and libraries

| Tool | Version / source | Role |
|---|---|---|
| nf-core/ampliseq [1, 2] | 2.18.0 (Nextflow [9], nf-core [10]) | upstream processing |
| DADA2 [3], VSEARCH [11] | in ampliseq | ASVs, 97% clustering, SILVA 138.2 taxonomy |
| QIIME 2 [5], q2-feature-classifier [12] | in ampliseq | SILVA 138 taxonomy |
| PICRUSt2 [6] | 2.6.3, PICRUSt2-SC [31] | functional prediction |
| phyloseq [13] | Bioconductor | data handling, rarefying |
| microViz [20] | r-universe | aggregation, diversity, ordination, PERMANOVA, bar plots |
| microbiome [21] | Bioconductor | evenness, rarity |
| vegan [22] | CRAN | rarefaction curves, adonis2, betadisper |
| ANCOMBC [23] | Bioconductor | ANCOM-BC2 |
| ggpicrust2 [24] | CRAN | KO → KEGG pathways |
